:::{#def-rank}
#### Rank

The **rank** of a matrix $\matr{A}$, written $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A})$,
is the largest number of columns of $\matr{A}$
that are linearly independent (@def-linearly-independent).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank}
#### The rank of two $3 \times 2$ matrices

The matrix
$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$
has rank $2$:
if $c_1 (1, 1, 1) + c_2 (1, 2, 3) = \vzero$,
then subtracting the first entry from the second gives $c_2 = 0$,
and then $c_1 = 0$.

The matrix
$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
has rank $1$:
its second column is twice its first,
so the two columns are not linearly independent,
but the first column on its own is.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-full-column-rank}
#### Full column rank

An $n \times p$ matrix has **full column rank**
if its rank (@def-rank) is $p$,
so that all of its columns are linearly independent.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-full-column-rank-shape}
#### Full column rank needs at least as many rows as columns

In @exm-rank, the first matrix has full column rank:
its rank is $2$, and it has $2$ columns.
The second does not, because its rank is $1$.

An $n \times p$ matrix can have full column rank only when $p \le n$,
because more than $n$ vectors of length $n$ are never linearly independent.
For example, the $2 \times 3$ matrix
$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
has $3$ columns of length $2$,
and $1 \cd (1, 0) + 1 \cd (0, 1) - 1 \cd (1, 1) = \vzero$,
with coefficients that are not all zero.
So its $3$ columns are not linearly independent,
and its rank is less than $3$.

:::
